l: interpreters, The Book of Mosiah
s: The interpreters are a gift from God: two stones fastened in bow rims, prepared to interpret languages and translate ancient records. Only a commanded seer may look in them; their possessor is called a seer. Preserved by the Lord to reveal iniquities, abominations, and mysteries, they are used by king Mosiah on plates of gold and later given to Alma the younger.

l: seer, The Book of Mosiah
s: A seer is a revelator and prophet who knows past and future things, reveals secret and hidden matters, makes unknown things known, and possesses interpreters after the manner of old times.

l: journey to find the land of Zarahemla, The Book of Mosiah
s: A journey by forty-three people seeking Zarahemla to obtain deliverance from bondage; they became lost for many days, found another land instead, and returned without reaching Zarahemla.

l: destruction of the people, The Book of Mosiah
s: affects people who had been destroyed [their cause was sought through translation of the records] The destruction of the people who had inhabited the discovered land is a subject Limhi wants to understand. He hopes the translated records will reveal its cause.

l: translation of the records, The Book of Mosiah
s: The records are translated by King Mosiah through interpreters after King Limhi desires their meaning. Their translation reveals an account of people who were destroyed, tracing from their destruction back to the great tower and the creation of Adam. It gives the people much knowledge and causes them to mourn.

l: bondage, The Book of Mosiah
s: King Laman intends to bring Zeniff’s people into bondage so that his people can benefit from the labor of their hands and the flocks of their fields. After twelve years, the threat of bondage contributes to the conflict between the peoples.

l: wars and contentions, The Book of Mosiah
s: occurs_in land of Nephi [between the Nephites and Lamanites] Wars and contentions begin in the land after king Laman stirs up his people against Zeniff’s people. The conflict includes an attack on Zeniff’s people and a battle in which the Lamanites are driven out.

l: Lamanite attack, The Book of Mosiah
s: A numerous Lamanite host attacks Zeniff’s people in the land of Shilom, slaying people and taking flocks and corn; after praying to God, Zeniff and his people defeat them.

l: Nephi, The Book of Mosiah
s: Nephi, favored because he faithfully keeps the Lord’s commandments, has prayers heard and answered, then obeys commands, leads a wilderness journey, and takes engraved records.

l: the people of Nephi, The Book of Mosiah
s: Descendants of Nephi, fewer than the people of Zarahemla, are eternally hated by Lamanites, who teach their children violence against them; they are later gathered with Zarahemla in two bodies.

l: land of Shemlon, The Book of Mosiah
s: Shemlon is a place hosting daughters of the Lamanites as they gather to sing, dance, and make merry.

l: possession of the land in peace, The Book of Mosiah
s: is_a state [of Zeniff's people] Zeniff and his people again begin to establish the kingdom and possess the land in peace. This peaceful possession lasts for twenty-two years before the Lamanites prepare to attack.

l: preparations for war, The Book of Mosiah
s: is_made_by Lamanites [against Zeniff's people] Zeniff causes weapons of every kind to be made and sets guards around the land to detect and prevent Lamanite attacks. After king Laman dies, his son stirs the Lamanites to rebellion and they prepare for war, while Zeniff’s spies discover their preparations.

l: battle against the Lamanites, The Book of Mosiah
s: is_fought_by Zeniff's people [with trust in the Lord] Zeniff’s people hide their women and children, gather their able men, arrange them by age, and go to battle against the Lamanites in the strength of the Lord. They contend face to face and drive the Lamanites out of the land.

l: slaughter of the Lamanites, The Book of Mosiah
s: is_caused_by Zeniff's people [great] Zeniff’s people slay the Lamanites with a great slaughter, killing so many that they do not number them. They then return to their own land.

l: Abinadi, The Book of Mosiah
s: Abinadi is a prophet among Noah’s people, commanded by the Lord and empowered by God’s Spirit to deliver a message to the priests and people. He first prophesies that the Lord will visit them in anger unless they repent, and is delivered when they seek his life. He later returns in disguise, condemns their hardened hearts and iniquity, is seized and imprisoned, and boldly rebukes king Noah and the priests. Protected from immediate death, he recites God’s commandments and teaches the law of Moses, salvation, the atonement, the Messiah, resurrection, and redemption through Christ. He testifies that God will come down, suffer, die, break death’s bands, and save his people. Refusing to deny his words or God’s commandments, Abinadi is bound, scourged, and killed by fire. Afterward, Alma teaches his words, which help form Alma’s church, while others mourn Abinadi’s death and remember his warning.

l: this people, The Book of Mosiah
s: The people under king Noah labor and are taxed to support Noah, his household, priests, and widespread iniquity. Deceived into idolatry, they delight in violence, boast after victory over the Lamanites, and reject Abinadi’s prophecy. They harden their hearts, refuse repentance, grow angry, seize Abinadi, and bring him before Noah, though they cannot harm him while the Spirit is upon him. Abinadi’s true words stand as testimony against their iniquities and foretell bondage, affliction, and destruction. Later, they pursue Alma’s people but cannot overtake them, and are linked to Alma’s people’s oppression and bondage.

l: priests of Noah, The Book of Mosiah
s: The priests of Noah are priests serving king Noah, installed after Noah replaces his father’s priests with men proud in heart. Supported by the people’s taxes, they practice laziness, idolatry, whoredoms, and lying and vain speech while claiming to teach the law of Moses and understand prophecy. They question and accuse Abinadi, advise Noah against releasing him, and help lead to his death. After fleeing into the wilderness, they abduct twenty-four daughters of the Lamanites, steal grain and precious things, and cause destruction that leads Limhi’s people to seek their punishment. Later, under Amulon, they oppress Alma’s people, bring them into iniquity, join the Lamanites, and possess and till the land of Amulon.

l: wickedness, The Book of Mosiah
s: Wickedness causes the Lord to send Abinadi to prophesy against Noah's people. Seen in their iniquities and abominations, it brings warnings to repent or face affliction, bondage, pestilence, and destruction.

l: whoredoms, The Book of Mosiah
s: Noah has many wives and concubines and causes the people to commit whoredoms. Noah's priests also spend their time with harlots, and Abinadi identifies the people's whoredoms as a reason for the Lord's warning.

l: victory over the Lamanites, The Book of Mosiah
s: causes pride [among Noah's people] Noah's armies are sent against the Lamanites and drive them back for a time. After the victory, Noah's people become proud, boast in their strength, and delight in the shedding of blood.

l: words of Abinadi, The Book of Mosiah
s: Abinadi’s words are a prophecy and testimony against king Noah and his people. They warn that unless the people repent and turn to the Lord, enemies will bring affliction and bondage, and the Lord will be slow to hear them. The words address their iniquity and the coming of God, are preserved by Alma, and are later fulfilled through suffering and bloodshed.

l: bondage, The Book of Mosiah
s: Bondage is the threatened state of Limhi’s people if Noah’s people refuse to repent: enemies afflict them, and only the Lord can deliver them. Their later deliverance is remembered with great joy and taught by Alma.

l: prayers, The Book of Mosiah
s: are_heard_by Lord [including Alma (father)'s prayers] The prayers of the people and of Alma (father) were heard by the Lord. The angel said that Alma (son) had been brought to the knowledge of the truth so that the prayers of the Lord’s servants might be answered according to their faith.

l: Zion, The Book of Mosiah
s: is_seen_eye_to_eye_by the watchmen of Zion [when the Lord brings again Zion] Zion is associated with the declaration that the Lord reigns. The Lord shall bring again Zion, and his watchmen shall see eye to eye when this occurs.

l: bonds of iniquity, The Book of Mosiah
s: Bonds of iniquity are a bondage from which Alma’s people are delivered. Iniquities are laid upon the Lord’s servant, bring affliction with diseases, are testified against by Abinadi, and are brought upon Alma’s people by King Noah and his priests.

l: Messiah, The Book of Mosiah
s: Messiah, prophesied by Moses and the prophets, comes among children of men in human form, is oppressed and afflicted, and brings resurrection of the dead.

l: redemption, The Book of Mosiah
s: Redemption is necessary for salvation: without it, all mankind would perish. Prepared from the foundation of the world, it satisfies justice and saves the Lord’s people from a lost and fallen state. It is made possible by Christ’s coming and comes through his power, sufferings, death, resurrection, and ascension. Though the children of Israel did not understand it because of hard hearts, Alma preached repentance and redemption. Alma (son) described being redeemed after repentance and tribulation, rescued from bitterness, iniquity, darkness, and eternal torment.

l: Isaiah, The Book of Mosiah
s: says report [as a prophetic witness] Isaiah is cited as declaring who has believed the report and to whom the arm of the Lord is revealed. His prophecy describes the servant’s appearance, suffering, death, offering for sin, and eventual portion with the great.

l: the Lord's servant, The Book of Mosiah
s: The Lord’s servant grows before the Lord as a tender plant and root from dry ground, without form or comeliness. Despised, rejected, sorrowful, oppressed, and afflicted, he silently goes to slaughter. He bears griefs, sorrows, transgressions, iniquities, and sins for others; is cut off, buried with the wicked and rich, yet has done no evil or deceit. His soul becomes an offering for sin, after which he has seed and prolonged days. By his knowledge he justifies many, intercedes for transgressors, and receives a portion with the great.

l: transgressions, The Book of Mosiah
s: are_borne_by the Lord's servant [ours] Transgressions cause the servant to be wounded and stricken. The servant bears the sins of many and makes intercession for transgressors.

l: death, The Book of Mosiah
s: Death is portrayed as the servant's self-pouring sacrifice, marked by burial among wicked and rich and being numbered with transgressors; Christ then breaks its bands, removes its victory and sting, swallows it up, and ends it through endless life.

l: the Father, The Book of Mosiah
s: The Father is identified with God because the Son was conceived by the power of God. The Son subjects the flesh and his will to the Father, and the Father and the Son are one God.

l: the seed of the Lord, The Book of Mosiah
s: is_a heirs of the kingdom of God [those who believe the prophets and look forward to remission of sins] The seed of the Lord consists of those who have heard and believed the words of the prophets, looked forward to the day of redemption, and those holy prophets who have prophesied. They are heirs of the kingdom of God.

l: the first resurrection, The Book of Mosiah
s: The first resurrection is the resurrection of those who lived before, live now, and will live until Christ’s resurrection. Brought to pass through Christ’s power, sufferings, and death, it provides eternal life and includes prophets, believers, commandment keepers, the ignorant without salvation declared, and little children, but excludes wilful rebels who die in sins.

l: bands of death, The Book of Mosiah
s: are_broken death [through the Son's victory] The Son breaks the bands of death and gains victory over death. Having broken them, he has power over the dead and brings to pass the resurrection of the dead.

l: carnality, The Book of Mosiah
s: keeps_in the fallen state [those who persist in their own carnal nature] Carnality keeps people in a fallen state when they persist in their own carnal nature and follow sin and rebellion against God. Such people are as though no redemption had been made and remain enemies to God.

l: Christ's coming into the world, The Book of Mosiah
s: enables redemption If Christ had not come into the world, there could have been no redemption.

l: the light of the world, The Book of Mosiah
s: is_endless endless [never darkened] Christ is the light of the world, an endless light that can never be darkened.

l: Alma, The Book of Mosiah
s: Alma is a young descendant of Nephi, formerly a priest of king Noah, whose belief in Abinadi’s words transforms him after he pleads with the king, is cast out and pursued, and hides to write Abinadi’s words. He repents of his sins and iniquities, teaches Abinadi’s words privately, and teaches believers repentance, redemption, and faith. With authority from God, he baptizes believers in the waters of Mormon, ordains priests, and forms the church of God through God’s strength and power and faith in Abinadi’s words. When king Noah’s army threatens them, Alma leads his people into the wilderness. As their beloved high priest, he teaches liberty, rejects kingship, consecrates just priests and teachers, teaches love of neighbors and avoidance of contention, and urges trust in the Lord. He leads people from bondage, preaches repentance and faith, teaches remembrance of the Lord’s deliverance, baptizes Limhi’s people, and receives power to establish churches and ordain priests and teachers. Later, as high priest with authority over the church from king Mosiah, he asks the Lord how to judge transgressors, records the Lord’s words, judges the accused, regulates church affairs, and continues teaching and serving despite afflictions.

l: seed, The Book of Mosiah
s: Abinadi says the seed of those who kill him will cause many believers in the Lord’s salvation to suffer death by fire.

l: death by fire, The Book of Mosiah
s: is_a pain [suffered by Abinadi and many of the seed] Death by fire is the manner in which Abinadi is put to death. He prophesies that the seed of those responsible will also suffer the pains of death by fire.

l: truth, The Book of Mosiah
s: Truth is sealed by Abinadi’s death, standing as testimony against king Noah and his people at the last day. An angel convinces Alma (son) of God’s power and authority, after which Alma and the sons of Mosiah teach truth through preaching and scriptures.

l: people who believed Alma, The Book of Mosiah
s: The people who believed Alma gather at Mormon, about two hundred and four souls, to hear him. They are baptized in the waters of Mormon, filled with grace, and covenant to serve God and keep his commandments. Called the church of God and church of Christ, they support one another and leave with Alma into the wilderness. Under Alma as high priest, the church admonishes sin, receives repentant believers through baptism, rejects those who will not hear the Lord’s voice, and gains peace, prosperity, and many baptized people.

l: Alma's people, The Book of Mosiah
s: Alma’s people, covenant believers led by Alma, have great faith and patience amid bondage, afflictions, persecution, tasks, task-masters, and guards. Warned of the king’s army, they depart with tents and families, endure strengthened burdens, travel through the wilderness, give thanks, and arrive in Zarahemla.

l: church of God, The Book of Mosiah
s: The church of God is a church formed by Alma and those with him through God’s strength, power, and faith in Abinadi’s words. Baptized people are added to it by God’s power and authority. Though composed of many churches, all are one church, preaching repentance and faith in God. It begins with baptism and formation, includes Limhi’s people waiting for authority, and later suffers persecution and dissension before Alma’s son and the sons of Mosiah repair injuries they caused.

l: church of Christ, The Book of Mosiah
s: is_a church [called the church of Christ] The baptized people were also called the church of Christ from that time forward. The church was taught to have unity, love, one faith, and one baptism.

l: priests, The Book of Mosiah
s: Priests taught believers about the kingdom of God, repentance, and faith on the Lord. Alma ordained one for every fifty people; they preached and taught, worked for their own support, and received God’s grace for their labor.

l: king's army, The Book of Mosiah
s: The king’s army was sent to destroy Alma and the people because the king accused Alma of stirring up rebellion. Alma and the people departed into the wilderness before the army arrived.

l: Mormon, The Book of Mosiah
s: Mormon is a place near the land’s borders, with waters, a pure fountain, thicket, and forest, where Alma taught believers and baptized about two hundred and four people.

l: waters of Mormon, The Book of Mosiah
s: The waters of Mormon, near the forest of Mormon, are a beautiful place where Alma baptized about two hundred and four people.

l: wilderness, The Book of Mosiah
s: receives departure into the wilderness [as the destination of Alma and the people of the Lord] The wilderness was the destination to which Alma and the people departed with their tents and families. They left Mormon to avoid the coming army of king Noah.

l: baptism, The Book of Mosiah
s: Baptism is a covenant and witness before the Lord of willingness to serve God and keep his commandments. Alma first baptizes Helam and other believers in the waters of Mormon. Limhi and many of his people later desire baptism, but it is delayed for lack of authority. Alma ultimately baptizes Limhi and all who desire it in the same manner.

l: commandments, The Book of Mosiah
s: include church gathering and worship [on the sabbath day and as often as possible] The people covenanted to keep God’s commandments. Alma also commanded them to avoid contention, observe the sabbath, give thanks, share their substance, and support those in need.

l: king's accusation of rebellion, The Book of Mosiah
s: concerns Alma [the king accused Alma of stirring up the people] The king accused Alma of stirring up the people to rebellion against him. Because of this accusation, he sent his army to destroy Alma and the people.

l: departure into the wilderness, The Book of Mosiah
s: A flight by Alma and the people of the Lord begins after warning that king Noah’s army will destroy them. About four hundred and fifty people take tents, families, flocks, and grain, then flee eight days into the wilderness.

l: knowledge of the Redeemer, The Book of Mosiah
s: is_gained_at Mormon [by those who came to the waters and forest] The place of Mormon, its waters, and its forest were described as beautiful to those who came there to the knowledge of their Redeemer. Those who gained this knowledge were described as blessed and as singing to his praise forever.

l: Gideon, The Book of Mosiah
s: Gideon is a strong man, enemy of king Noah, captain, and servant of king Limhi. He fights and pursues Noah but spares him when the Lamanites appear. He counsels Limhi against punishing his people, identifies Noah’s priests, and devises an escape: wine for the guards and a secret pass from bondage.

l: king of the Lamanites, The Book of Mosiah
s: The king of the Lamanites receives Nephite tribute and leads the Lamanites in war. He swears with Limhi that his people will not slay Limhi’s people, takes tribute, and stations guards. Later, wounded and captured while attacking Limhi’s people, he learns priests caused an abduction, is pacified, and returns peacefully.

l: wilderness, The Book of Mosiah
s: A wilderness traversed by Alma’s people and entered by Zarahemla’s people with Mulek. Alma’s people flee there for eight days from king Noah, later depart after escaping bondage and travel twelve days to Zarahemla; pursuing Lamanites become lost.

l: tribute to the king of the Lamanites, The Book of Mosiah
s: Tribute to the king of the Lamanites is paid yearly by Nephites, amounting to half their possessions and supporting guards set around the land.

l: invasion of the land of Shemlon, The Book of Mosiah
s: is_conducted_by Lamanites The army of the Lamanites comes within the borders of the land of Shemlon while Gideon is pursuing king Noah. The invasion causes king Noah and his people to flee into the wilderness.

l: flight into the wilderness, The Book of Mosiah
s: King Noah commands the people to flee before the Lamanites, and they leave with their women and children. He later commands the men to leave their families, causing some to flee while others remain with their families.

l: capture of king Noah's people, The Book of Mosiah
s: Lamanites overtake king Noah’s people in the land of Nephi, slay some, spare others, take them captive, and demand king Noah under tribute.

l: death of king Noah, The Book of Mosiah
s: is_caused_by Gideon [by fire after the people turned against him] King Noah’s people find him in the wilderness without his priests. After he commands them not to return, they become angry and cause him to suffer death by fire.

l: oath between the Lamanite king and Limhi, The Book of Mosiah
s: Oath between the Lamanite king and Limhi’s people promises they will not be slain; Limhi says his people kept it, but the king attacks believing they took daughters.

l: establishment of Limhi's kingdom, The Book of Mosiah
s: is_conducted_by Limhi The people confer the kingdom upon Limhi after returning to the land of Nephi. Limhi begins to establish the kingdom while his people pay tribute to the king of the Lamanites.

l: peace among Limhi's people, The Book of Mosiah
s: Limhi establishes peace among his people, who enjoy two continual years without Lamanite molestation or destruction.

l: the daughters of the Lamanites, The Book of Mosiah
s: The daughters of the Lamanites gather in Shemlon to sing, dance, and make merry; twenty-four are carried into the wilderness and marry Amulon’s children and brethren.

l: war, The Book of Mosiah
s: War between the Lamanites and people of Limhi begins over abducted daughters and ends when the Lamanite king is pacified.

l: battle, The Book of Mosiah
s: The battle between the Lamanites and the people of Limhi becomes exceedingly sore. The people of Limhi drive the Lamanites back despite being fewer in number.

l: abduction of the daughters, The Book of Mosiah
s: The priests of king Noah abduct twenty-four daughters of the Lamanites into the wilderness, causing the Lamanites to attack the people of Limhi.

l: Lamanite attack on the people of Limhi, The Book of Mosiah
s: Believing their daughters were abducted, Lamanites attack to destroy Limhi’s people, who defeat them and capture their wounded king.

l: pacification, The Book of Mosiah
s: Pacification follows Limhi’s explanation that priests abducted daughters; the Lamanite king and people accept it, meet Limhi’s people unarmed, and return peacefully.

l: the people of Limhi’s defense, The Book of Mosiah
s: The people of Limhi defend against the Lamanites, using waiting places to attack; though fewer, they fight for their families and drive the Lamanites before them.

l: Ammon's brethren, The Book of Mosiah
s: is_from Zarahemla [with Ammon] Ammon’s brethren come with him from Zarahemla and are initially bound and cast into prison after being mistaken for the priests of Noah. They mourn the deaths caused by Noah and his priests and the departure of Alma and the people who went with him.

l: Alma's brethren, The Book of Mosiah
s: Alma's brethren are the people who fled with Alma into the wilderness after forming a church of God. Taught and led by Alma, they settle in the land of Helam, prosper with flocks and grain, and build its city. Captured by the Lamanites and placed under guards, they are ultimately delivered from bondage by the power of God and become free in liberty.

l: record of the destroyed people, The Book of Mosiah
s: A record engraved on ore plates tells of people whose bones were found; it is recovered and sent to Mosiah for interpretation.

l: battles against the Lamanites, The Book of Mosiah
s: causes destruction of Limhi's people [through repeated defeats and loss of life] Limhi’s people go against the Lamanites three times after complaining of their afflictions. They are beaten and driven back each time, suffering much loss and many deaths.

l: destruction of Limhi's people, The Book of Mosiah
s: creates widows of Limhi's people [because many men were slain] The destruction of Limhi’s people includes many men being slain in battle, leaving a great number of widows and causing mourning and lamentation throughout the land.

l: afflictions of the Nephites, The Book of Mosiah
s: causes people of Limhi [to murmur and seek battle] The afflictions of the Nephites are great because the Lamanites surround them on every side and there is no way for them to deliver themselves. Their afflictions lead them to murmur, battle, humble themselves, and cry to God.

l: gift from God to interpret engravings, The Book of Mosiah
s: belongs_to king Mosiah [enabling him to interpret engravings] The gift from God to interpret engravings is possessed by king Mosiah. Ammon tells Limhi about this gift, which allows Mosiah to interpret the engravings on the plates of ore.

l: the wilderness, The Book of Mosiah
s: The people of Limhi travel through the wilderness with their families, flocks, herds, provisions, and precious things. The Lamanites pursue them into the wilderness but lose their tracks and become lost.

l: the voice of the people, The Book of Mosiah
s: chooses judges [as the basis for conducting public business] The voice of the people first calls for Aaron to be king and later chooses judges. Mosiah teaches that the people should conduct their business by this voice.

l: the escape of the people of Limhi, The Book of Mosiah
s: passes_through the back pass [by night] The escape of the people of Limhi occurs by night after the Lamanites drink the wine sent by king Limhi. The people travel around the land of Shilom through the wilderness and reach the land of Zarahemla.

l: the journey to Zarahemla, The Book of Mosiah
s: passes_around the land of Shilom [through the wilderness] The journey to Zarahemla takes the people of Limhi many days through the wilderness. They are led by Ammon and his brethren and arrive with their families, herds, flocks, provisions, and precious things.

l: Amulon, The Book of Mosiah
s: Amulon leads king Noah’s priests, pleads with the Lamanites for their lives, and joins them. Granted rule over his people in Helam, he gains favor with king Laman, teaches the Lamanites, exercises authority over Alma, and persecutes Alma’s people through task-masters and their children.

l: the brethren of Alma, The Book of Mosiah
s: Brethren of Alma possess Helam, flee into its city as Lamanites appear, pray, surrender, and become subject to Lamanite guards.

l: the land of Helam, The Book of Mosiah
s: Helam is a beautiful, pleasant land with pure water where Alma’s people settle, cultivate, build, and prosper before the Lamanites take possession.

l: the city of Helam, The Book of Mosiah
s: Helam is a city built in the land of Helam by Alma’s people, who gather there when the Lamanites appear.

l: the bondage of king Noah and his priests, The Book of Mosiah
s: The bondage of king Noah and his priests oppresses Alma’s people through iniquity, continues under Amulon and task-masters, and ends when God delivers Alma and his people and leads them into the wilderness.

l: liberty, The Book of Mosiah
s: Liberty is freedom given by God to Alma’s people and granted through judges; Alma urges them to stand fast and reject a king, while the Lamanites break their promise, and the people rejoice after choosing judges.

l: the deliverance of Alma’s people, The Book of Mosiah
s: The deliverance of Alma’s people is the Lord’s rescue of them through God’s power: they escape king Noah, are released from iniquity and bondage to the Lamanites, rejoice greatly, and are taught by Alma to remember it.

l: the Lamanite capture of Helam, The Book of Mosiah
s: is_a capture [of the land of Helam] The Lamanite capture of Helam occurs after the Lord softens the Lamanites’ hearts and Alma and his brethren surrender. The Lamanites take possession of the land and set guards over Alma and his brethren.

l: the founding of the church, The Book of Mosiah
s: Alma establishes a church among the people, is blessed, and the Lord promises it and its people will be established as his.

l: brethren of Amulon, The Book of Mosiah
s: The brethren of Amulon are appointed teachers over the Lamanites, teaching Nephi’s language, record keeping, and writing while withholding God, the law of Moses, and Abinadi’s words.

l: records, The Book of Mosiah
s: Records include brass, Nephi, and gold plates; King Mosiah preserves and translates them, then gives records and interpreters to Alma the younger to keep for future generations.

l: afflictions, The Book of Mosiah
s: is_a condition [experienced by Alma and his people] The afflictions of Alma and his people become so great that they cry mightily to God. Their afflictions are the setting in which God visits them, strengthens them, and promises deliverance.

l: burdens, The Book of Mosiah
s: is_lightened_by God [for Alma and his brethren] The burdens laid upon Alma and his brethren are made light by God. God strengthens them so that they can bear their burdens with ease even while in bondage.

l: valley Alma, The Book of Mosiah
s: A wilderness valley named for Alma after he led his people there; they camp and give thanks, then God tells Alma to leave as Lamanites pursue them.

l: the people, The Book of Mosiah
s: The people were gathered, heard the records read, and experienced joy, sorrow, gratitude, and anguish. They were taught repentance and faith, and many joined the churches of God.

l: the records of Zeniff, The Book of Mosiah
s: A record of Zeniff’s people, recounting their departure from Zarahemla through their eventual return.

l: the children of Amulon and his brethren, The Book of Mosiah
s: The children of Amulon and his brethren reject their fathers’ name, marry Lamanite daughters, and take Nephi’s name to be numbered among the Nephites.

l: churches, The Book of Mosiah
s: Seven churches in Zarahemla have priests and teachers; Alma establishes them to teach repentance and faith in God, uniting them as one church.

l: faith in God, The Book of Mosiah
s: is_preached the people [throughout the churches] The churches preached faith in God, and the people were taught repentance and faith.

l: the reading of the records, The Book of Mosiah
s: is_performed_by king Mosiah [for the assembled people] King Mosiah caused the records of Zeniff and the account of Alma and his brethren to be read, and the people responded with wonder, joy, sorrow, gratitude, and anguish.

l: the establishment of churches, The Book of Mosiah
s: is_authorized_by king Mosiah [with power given to Alma] King Mosiah granted Alma power to establish churches throughout the land of Zarahemla and to ordain priests and teachers over every church.

l: preaching repentance and faith, The Book of Mosiah
s: is_performed_by Alma [on the Lord] Alma preached repentance and faith on the Lord, and the priests preached the word as it was delivered to them by Alma. The churches preached only repentance and faith in God.

l: rising generation, The Book of Mosiah
s: The rising generation, once little children during king Benjamin's speech, becomes a separate people in faith. Unbelief leaves them unable to understand the word of God; with hardened hearts, they reject their fathers' traditions, resurrection, Christ, baptism, the Lord, and church membership.

l: word of God, The Book of Mosiah
s: The word of God is taught by Alma and fellow laborers to hardened unbelievers, then the sons of Mosiah seek to impart it to the Lamanites by journeying to preach among them.

l: people of God, The Book of Mosiah
s: People belonging to God bear the Lord’s name, receive forgiveness through repentance, and remain fewer than unbelievers as dissensions multiply them.

l: transgressors, The Book of Mosiah
s: Transgressors are judged by their sins; those who confess and sincerely repent are forgiven and received into the church, while those refusing repentance are not numbered among the people.

l: forgiveness, The Book of Mosiah
s: Forgiveness is freely granted by Lord to believers who confess and sincerely repent; among people it is required when a neighbor repents, and refusal brings condemnation.

l: unbelievers, The Book of Mosiah
s: persecute church of God [before the proclamation of king Mosiah] Unbelievers inflicted persecutions on the church and caused many people to be led astray. They later persecuted Alma (son) and those with him while they preached the word of God.

l: persecutions, The Book of Mosiah
s: is_a affliction of the church [inflicted by unbelievers] Persecutions inflicted by unbelievers became so great that the church complained to its leaders. King Mosiah then issued a proclamation against such persecution.

l: Alma (father of Alma the younger), The Book of Mosiah
s: Alma, father of Alma the younger, reports persecutions to king Mosiah and faithfully prays for his son’s knowledge of truth. After his son’s angelic appearance, he rejoices and gathers witnesses; later, his son receives records and interpreters from king Mosiah.

l: people, The Book of Mosiah
s: The people practice equality and neighborly esteem, prosper into a large, wealthy, peaceful population that spreads and builds settlements, are led astray by Alma, then many return to truth through Alma and Mosiah’s sons.

l: equality among all men, The Book of Mosiah
s: is_desired_in land [especially among Mosiah's people] Mosiah desires that inequality be no more in the land, especially among his people, and the people seek an equal chance throughout the land.

l: Alma the younger, The Book of Mosiah
s: Alma the younger begins as an unbelieving, wicked, idolatrous man who flatters people into dissension, steals hearts from the church of God, and seeks its destruction. After an angelic rebuke, he repents, is born of God, beholds God’s marvelous light, and is redeemed despite having rejected and denied the Redeemer. Made a new creature, he preaches the word of God throughout the land despite persecution. King Mosiah gives him the plates, records, and interpreters, commanding him to preserve them, record the people, and pass them from generation to generation.

l: sons of Mosiah, The Book of Mosiah
s: The sons of Mosiah begin as unbelievers who secretly seek to destroy the church with Alma (son). After an angelic appearance, they suffer anguish for their iniquities, confess, repair injuries to the church, teach God’s commandments, and publish truth and good tidings, bringing many to knowledge of truth. They desire salvation for every creature, decline the kingdom, and ask king Mosiah to let them preach the word of God among the Lamanites. With selected companions, they go to the land of Nephi, hoping the Lamanites abandon hatred, rejoice in the Lord, and become friendly with the Nephites.

l: angel of the Lord, The Book of Mosiah
s: An angelic appearance sent from God appears in a cloud to Alma (son) and his companions, speaks with thunderous power that shakes the earth, rebukes Alma, testifies of God’s authority, and commands him to cease persecuting the church.

l: church persecution, The Book of Mosiah
s: is_prohibited throughout the land [by proclamation of king Mosiah] Church persecution became severe enough that the church complained to its leaders. King Mosiah responded by forbidding unbelievers from persecuting members of the church of God.

l: angelic appearance, The Book of Mosiah
s: shakes land [with a voice as thunder] The angelic appearance caused Alma (son) and those with him to fall to the earth in astonishment. Alma (son) became unable to speak or move until the people fasted and prayed for him.

l: fasting and prayer, The Book of Mosiah
s: The priests assembled and fasted and prayed for two days and two nights that Alma (son) would speak and regain the strength of his limbs. Afterward, his limbs received their strength and he began to speak.

l: conversion of Alma, The Book of Mosiah
s: Alma's conversion begins with an angel confronting his persecution, leads to repentance, spiritual rebirth and redemption, and ends with him teaching others.

l: Redeemer, The Book of Mosiah
s: makes_manifest Second Coming of Christ [to every creature] Alma (son) said that he had rejected his Redeemer but later came to know that the Redeemer would come and make himself manifest unto all. He taught that every knee would bow and every tongue confess before him.

l: preaching the word of God, The Book of Mosiah
s: is_persecuted by unbelievers [with smiting] Alma and those who were with him traveled throughout the land preaching the word of God amid much tribulation and persecution. Their teaching consoled the church, confirmed its faith, and brought many to the knowledge of the truth.

l: Ammon, The Book of Mosiah
s: is_a son of Mosiah [one of the four] Ammon was one of the four sons of Mosiah who traveled through the lands under king Mosiah. He helped confess their sins, explain the prophecies and scriptures, and bring many to the knowledge of the truth.

l: Aaron, The Book of Mosiah
s: Aaron, a son of Mosiah, is named the people’s desired king and ruler, but while in the land of Nephi he declines to take the kingdom.

l: request to preach among the Lamanites, The Book of Mosiah
s: The sons of Mosiah plead with king Mosiah for many days to go to the land of Nephi with selected companions and preach the word of God among the Lamanites. King Mosiah asks the Lord about the request, receives permission, and grants it.

l: people, The Book of Mosiah
s: The people initially desire a king, but after Mosiah’s words relinquish that wish, choose judges by collective voice, seek equal chances throughout the land, and accept responsibility for their sins.

l: king, The Book of Mosiah
s: A ruler whose wickedness can bring sin, destruction, bondage, wars, and bloodshed; Mosiah warns the people, who ultimately choose no king.

l: wars, The Book of Mosiah
s: are a cause of bloodshed [among the people] Mosiah warns that disputes over kingship could cause wars, and he describes wars as part of the destruction caused by an unrighteous king.

l: bloodshed, The Book of Mosiah
s: is destructive [resulting from wars and contentions] Mosiah warns that contentions over kingship could cause much bloodshed and describes bloodshed as an effect of an unrighteous king.

l: judges, The Book of Mosiah
s: Mosiah proposes judges under the law; the people appoint them throughout the land, where higher and lower judges judge one another by the people’s voice.

l: chief judge, The Book of Mosiah
s: Chief judge is the highest judge, first held by Alma, who is appointed and judges righteously while keeping God’s commandments.

l: laws, The Book of Mosiah
s: Mosiah directs the people to be judged by ancestral laws, declaring them correct and given by the Lord.

l: Alma, The Book of Mosiah
s: Alma, Zarahemla’s first chief judge and church high priest, keeps the commandments, judges righteously, and presides during continual peace.

l: rights and privileges, The Book of Mosiah
s: are_enjoyed_by people [alike, while the Lord permits them to inherit the land] Mosiah desires that every person may enjoy rights and privileges alike for as long as the Lord allows the people and their posterity to inherit the land.

l: reign of the judges, The Book of Mosiah
s: begins_with Alma [as first and chief judge] The reign of the judges begins throughout the land of Zarahemla after the people appoint judges, with Alma as the first and chief judge.

l: reign of the kings, The Book of Mosiah
s: ends Mosiah [among the people of Nephi] The reign of the kings ends among the people of Nephi after the people relinquish their desire for a king.

l: appointment of judges, The Book of Mosiah
s: is_based_on voice of the people [throughout the land] The people assemble throughout the land and cast their voices to appoint judges who will judge them according to the law.

l: Mosiah's written message, The Book of Mosiah
s: Mosiah’s written message warns that unjust kings bring dangers and burdens, argues against kingship, and supports appointing judges under the fathers’ laws.

l: death of Mosiah, The Book of Mosiah
s: occurs_during reign of the kings [in the thirty and third year of his reign] Mosiah dies in the thirty and third year of his reign at sixty and three years old, after the people have chosen judges.

l: end of the reign of the kings, The Book of Mosiah
s: occurs_before reign of the judges [in the transition of government] The reign of the kings ends after Mosiah’s message convinces the people to relinquish their desire for a king and appoint judges instead.

l: The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: This record recounts the reign of the judges among the people of Nephi, centered on Alma’s religious leadership, missionary work, and later wars for liberty. After Mosiah’s death, Alma judges Nehor for priestcraft and murder, then leads the Nephites against Amlici and the Lamanites. Though wars bring great loss, the church is restored; later pride, inequality, and persecution cause Alma to give up the judgment-seat to Nephihah and devote himself to preaching repentance, faith in Jesus Christ, humility, care for the poor, and preparation for judgment. Alma ministers in Zarahemla, Gideon, Melek, Ammonihah, and Sidom. With Amulek, he confronts Ammonihah’s wickedness, Zeezrom’s accusations, and teachings that deny God. Alma and Amulek teach Christ’s redemption, resurrection, justice, mercy, repentance, and priesthood. Believers are burned and Alma and Amulek imprisoned, but they are delivered; Ammonihah is later destroyed, while Sidom prospers in faith. The account follows the sons of Mosiah among the Lamanites. Ammon serves king Lamoni and helps convert him; Aaron converts Lamoni’s father. Thousands become the Anti-Nephi-Lehies, bury their weapons rather than shed blood, suffer massacre, and later find Nephite refuge in Jershon as the people of Ammon. Alma counters Korihor’s anti-Christ teachings, then ministers among poor Zoramites with Amulek, teaching faith as a seed, Christ’s atonement, continual prayer, and urgent repentance. Alma counsels Helaman, Shiblon, and Corianton, entrusting sacred records to Helaman and explaining conversion, resurrection, restoration, justice, mercy, and the atonement. War then dominates the account: Moroni defends Nephite liberty, lands, families, and worship against Amalickiah, Ammoron, dissenters, and Lamanite armies. He creates the title of liberty, fortifies cities, wins battles with Lehi, Teancum, Helaman, and others, and confronts governmental neglect. Helaman’s two thousand and sixty sons of the people of Ammon fight faithfully and survive despite wounds. After Pahoran and Moroni reclaim Zarahemla from rebels, the Lamanites are driven from the land, peace and the church are restored, and Helaman dies. The record closes with transfers of sacred things, Moroni’s and Shiblon’s deaths, Hagoth’s voyages northward, renewed Lamanite conflict, and the ending of the account of Alma, Helaman, and Shiblon.

l: Mosiah, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Mosiah, last king of the people of Nephi and Ammon’s father, establishes accepted laws, dies upright after a good warfare, and leaves no successor.

l: Alma, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Alma is a Nephite leader, judge, governor, chief judge, high priest, preacher, teacher, and righteous man. He begins by reigning in the judgment-seat, judging Nehor for priestcraft and killing Gideon. As chief judge and governor, he leads Nephite armies against the Amlicites and Lamanites, kills Amlici, and preserves his people. Consecrated a high priest by his father, he receives revelation and prophecy through the Spirit, preaches repentance, rebirth, righteousness, and the coming of Jesus Christ, and organizes the church by ordaining priests and elders and establishing churches in many lands. He teaches in Gideon, Melek, Ammonihah, Sidom, Zarahemla, and among the Zoramites. Rejected from Ammonihah, he returns by divine command, fasts, stays with Amulek, testifies boldly, and later helps Zeezrom, establishes a church in Sidom, and administers to Amulek. Alma rejoices with the sons of Mosiah, leads companions among the Zoramites, prays for their strength, and teaches the poor in heart that faith can begin as an experiment upon the word and grow like a seed into a tree. He has sons Helaman, Shiblon, and Corianton. Near the end, he teaches and blesses Helaman and his other sons, prophesies concerning the people of Nephi, blesses the land and church, then departs from Zarahemla; his death and burial are unknown.

l: Nehor, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Nehor is a large, very strong man who preaches false doctrines, including universal salvation and paid priests. He gains followers, money, and costly apparel and establishes a church. After killing Gideon with a sword, he is condemned to death under Mosiah’s law and acknowledges the word of God before dying.

l: Gideon, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Gideon, a church of God teacher, speaks God’s words against Nehor, helps deliver Limhi’s people from bondage, and is slain by Nehor’s sword.

l: God, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: God is the one true and living deity, Supreme Creator of all things in heaven and earth, creator of the people, and Lord, Redeemer, Great Spirit, Most High God, and God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. God has all power, wisdom, understanding, and knowledge of thoughts and appointed times; his course is one eternal round, his paths are straight, his decrees and promises do not vary, and his judgments are just. God gives commandments, reveals the plan of redemption, sends angels and spiritual knowledge, ordains priests, calls teachers, and gives the Holy Ghost, power, faith, strength, blessings, liberty, and protection. God is merciful toward those who call on and believe in his name, repent, and bring forth righteousness: he forgives sins, removes guilt, hears prayer everywhere, comforts and supports people in affliction, delivers them from bondage and enemies, and promises resurrection and salvation through his Son, who will come and atone for the sins of the world. God also judges every person according to deeds, cannot allow continuing iniquity, and cuts off or destroys those who persist in wickedness. Across the records, God marks, blesses, curses, preserves, directs, and prospers peoples according to their response to his commandments; he repeatedly delivers the faithful, especially the Nephites, their fathers, Ammon's brethren, and the sons of the people of Ammon. Worship, prayer, covenants, repentance, preaching, and trust in God form the response invited from people, while God works even through small means to fulfill eternal purposes.

l: Christ, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Christ is Jesus Christ, the Son of God and Only Begotten of the Father, described as full of grace, mercy, truth, and other divine qualities. He is central to redemption: he comes to take away the sins of the world, takes upon himself the transgressions of his people, and atones through his sufferings, death, and infinite, eternal sacrifice. His redemption and salvation are offered to those who believe on his name, including those baptized unto repentance, and mercy through him brings peace and remission of sins. He breaks the bands of death, has victory over death, brings about the resurrection, and makes restoration of soul and body requisite. His coming is foreseen in the law of Moses, prophesied by prophets, awaited by believers, taught by Alma and Aaron, and denied by Korihor and the Zoramites. Individuals and communities place faith, hope, prayer, healing, comfort, and joy in him; he saves the queen from an awful hell, comforts Alma’s companions, and redeems those who die firmly believing. He is also called the Redeemer, the life, light, word of truth, and righteousness of the world, the only way to salvation, and the one who will preside at judgment after resurrection. The records move from identifying his nature and promised coming, through teachings about his atoning work and victory over death, to its effects in belief, repentance, comfort, resurrection, redemption, and salvation.

l: people of Nephi, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The people of Nephi are a people in the land of Zarahemla, ruled by judges and maintaining a free government. They accept Mosiah’s laws, enforce them as far as possible, and use the voice of the people to reject Amlici as king and later settle disputes over the law and Pahoran. They experience both prosperity and peace and persecution, conflict, invasion, and losses caused by the Lamanites. Some become proud, contentious, unequal, and persecuting, while others aid the poor and needy. They establish the church of God more fully, many are baptized in Sidon, and the church becomes generally established after an invasion and years of peace. Highly favored by the Lord, they receive light, knowledge, deliverance, prosperity, the Spirit, prophecy, revelation, and spiritual gifts. Moroni strengthens and teaches them to defend themselves without offense; they rejoice in deliverance and Helaman’s success, giving thanks, fasting, praying, and worshipping. Yet Alma warns that despite their blessings, rebellion could bring destruction; after Jesus Christ manifests himself to them, they dwindle in unbelief and ultimately become extinct through wars, pestilences, famines, and bloodshed.

l: judges, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Judges were selected to judge crimes, ruled the people of Nephi, received wages by time labored, enforced debts, and judged by law and evidence. Some lawyers and judges stirred up disturbances to gain cases and earnings, laying a foundation for the people’s destruction.

l: church of God, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The church of God is a church belonging to God, named after Christ because its members take upon themselves his name. It shares the word of God freely, prohibits persecution, gives to the poor, needy, sick, and afflicted without respect to persons, and remains neat without costly apparel. Though persecuted and tried by contention, it can be steadfast in faith, peaceful, and prosperous without setting its heart on riches. It is established in Zarahemla, the land of Zarahemla, the land of Mormon, and throughout the land, with high priests who care for it. Its course includes threats from Nehor and Amlici; restoration, labor, generosity, and prosperity; fuller establishment and thousands joining through baptism; then pride, envy, strife, malice, and persecution among members, which hinder its progress and become a stumbling-block to unbelievers. Alma is warned to cease seeking its destruction. Later, Helaman and his brethren care for it, maintain order, preach with power, bring many to repentance and baptism, and establish it again throughout the land.

l: priests, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Priests are ordained servants and preachers who preside over the church. They leave labor to impart God’s word, then diligently return to it, remaining equal to hearers and learners. They teach commandments and redemption, preach repentance throughout the land, condemn many sins, and teach the coming, sufferings, death, and resurrection of the Son of God.

l: law of Mosiah, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The law established by Mosiah governs the people of Nephi, requiring obedience and punishing liars, thieves, robbers, and murderers. It provides judges, their wages, reckoning, and measures; directs judgment of transgressors; and requires matters such as establishing a king to be decided by the voice of the people.

l: word of God, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The word of God is a liberal message made available to all, without price or exclusion, through assemblies, churches, priests, teachers, streets, houses, synagogues, and preaching throughout the land. It is declared according to revelation, taught in purity, and spoken in nations’ own nation and tongue. It fulfills prophecy, including the prophecy concerning the mark, the curse, and those who fight against Nephi and his seed; the Amlicites fulfill it by marking their foreheads. Its central power is to deliver from bondage, illuminate darkened souls, pull down pride, craftiness, and contentions, convince people of sins and incorrect traditions, and affect minds more powerfully than the sword. It calls people to repentance, establishes consequences such as death, judgment, and iniquity, and will not be void. Yet resistance hardens hearts, gives people a lesser portion, and can leave them without knowledge of God’s mysteries. Those who believe it may face being cast out, stoned, burned, or expelled from their land, while opponents such as the more popular Zoramites reject it because it destroys their craft. The word is received with joy by prepared people and is presented as a seed to be planted in hearts, tested for goodness, and nourished by faith. As it grows, it enlarges the soul, enlightens understanding, expands the mind, becomes a tree, and leads through the Son of God unto salvation and everlasting life.

l: priestcraft, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Priestcraft is introduced among people of Nephi by Nehor, enforced by sword, threatens destruction if enforced, and continues spreading through false doctrines.

l: faith in Christ, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Faith in Christ is steadfast belief and hope in things not seen but true, rather than perfect knowledge. It begins by being taught, received through words, and given place in the heart. As people experiment upon, plant, and diligently nourish the word with patience and care, faith increases. It is joined with the spirit of prophecy, repentance, good works, continual prayer, and obedience. Faith leads people to repentance, brings about redemption, supports the great and eternal plan of redemption, and offers hope unto eternal salvation; without faith unto repentance, people remain exposed to the demands of justice. It also brings mighty changes of heart and remission of sins, enables knowledge of mysteries, and can help bring many souls to repentance. Faith on Jesus Christ withstands temptation, while faith in God brings guidance and miracles. The records show it in Alma's father, the queen, Ammon, Melchizedek, the Lamanites, the righteous church, and the two thousand and sixty. It brings preservation and deliverance to those who do not doubt, stand fast, and obey, and cannot be destroyed by force.

l: persecution, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Persecution concerns affliction of humble church members, initially by outsiders using words and arising amid contention. Later, some church members persecute nonbelievers according to their will, while humble followers of God continue suffering from the remainder of the people.

l: judgment-seat, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The judgment-seat is the office held by the chief judge. Alma delivers it to Nephihah, who judges and governs until his death; his son Pahoran then fills it. Pahoran keeps it after the king-men fail to remove him, though rebels led by Pachus take it. Pahoran seeks it only to preserve his people’s rights and liberty, is restored after Pachus is slain, and returns after the wars.

l: reign of the judges, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The reign of the judges governs the people of Nephi after Mosiah’s death, beginning with Alma in the judgment-seat. Its early years include peace through the fifth year, while later years bring wars, contentions, and many deaths; it continues through the nineteenth year.

l: death of Gideon, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: is_caused_by sword [Nehor is the killer] Gideon, being advanced in years and unable to withstand Nehor’s blows, is slain by the sword. Nehor is then taken by the people of the church and brought before Alma.

l: execution of Nehor, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: occurs_on hill Manti [where Nehor suffered an ignominious death] Nehor is condemned according to the law acknowledged by the people. He is carried to the top of hill Manti, acknowledges that his teachings oppose the word of God, and suffers an ignominious death.

l: peace, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Peace returns as church members remain steady, labor, and share with the needy, bringing much peace among the people of Nephi. After the Lamanites are driven out, continual peace lasts three years. It begins throughout the land of Zarahemla in the sixteenth year of the reign of the judges and continues into the seventeenth.

l: prosperity, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Prosperity is exceedingly great riches from heed, diligence, faithfulness, and security. Church members and Nephites gain abundant flocks, herds, grain, precious metals, silk, linen, and strength, then use prosperous circumstances to provide for those in need.

l: humility, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: leads_to repentance [when a person is compelled to be humble] Those who are lowly in heart are blessed. Being compelled to be humble can lead a person to seek repentance, while those who humble themselves without compulsion are more blessed.

l: pride, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Pride afflicts some church members, arising from riches, worldly possessions, and costly apparel, and should be avoided. Nehor is lifted up and others become proud and contend. Later, wealth and fine clothing foster scorn, persecution, contentions, and decline. The Zoramites end with hearts lifted up in boasting, puffed up by vain worldly things.

l: riches, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Riches are sought by Nehor through false preaching, while church members become rich without setting their hearts on them and give liberally to those in need.

l: swords, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Swords are weapons alongside cimeters and bows, used by Nehor to kill Gideon and later surrendered by Lamanites under compulsion or covenant. Anti-Nephi-Lehi retain and bury brightened swords as testimony of ending their use. Zerahemnah delivers, receives back, and ultimately loses weapons; Moroni commands further Lamanite surrender, binding those who resist.

l: riches, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The Zoramites' hearts were set upon gold, silver, costly apparel, ringlets, bracelets, ornaments of gold, and other precious things. Their desire for these fine goods accompanied their boasting and worship.

l: labor, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Nehor teaches that priests and teachers should not labor with their hands but should be supported by the people. In the church, priests and hearers return diligently to their labors, and everyone labors according to strength.

l: wickedness, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Wickedness is a stumbling-block to those outside the church and never happiness. When people fall into it, it causes loss of freedom, sorrow, inequality, death, destruction, and afflictions. The church’s wickedness led unbelievers from one iniquity to another and hindered the church’s progress. Alma grieved over the iniquity of the Zoramites and sought help to bear its effects; a son’s conduct brought great iniquity upon them and required repentance. The people are warned that transgression and forsaking God bring destruction through their own actions.

l: Amlici, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Amlici is a cunning, worldly-wise, wicked man who follows Nehor’s order, draws people after him, and seeks kingship. Rejected by the people, he is made king by supporters, leads them to take arms against their brethren and destroy the church of God, and is killed by Alma.

l: church, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The church is established in Zarahemla under its prior order, with priests and teachers appointed throughout the land. It receives repentant, baptized people, while unrepentant members are rejected and removed. Alma establishes its order in Gideon, though Ammonihah rejects its traditions. Alma blesses the faithful, and Helaman and his brethren reestablish the church amid dissension from those who refuse their words.

l: Amlicites, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The Amlicites are a people and Amlici’s followers, distinguished by his name. Armed for war and led by appointed rulers, they fight the Nephites, join the Lamanites, and are defeated and pursued into the wilderness. Fighting alongside the Lamanites, they suffer 12,532 slain, mark their foreheads red, rebel openly against God, and bring a curse upon themselves.

l: Nephites, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The Nephites are a people of God and of Nephi, identified by belief in records brought from Jerusalem, correct ancestral traditions, and keeping God’s commandments. They keep true records, follow their own reckoning and measure, and occupy Zarahemla, Bountiful, and much of the land northward while hemming the Lamanites into the south. Their central story is repeated defense of their lands, homes, families, liberty, rights, religion, and worship against the Lamanites and internal dissensions. They arm themselves, appoint captains, fortify cities, and fight reluctantly when necessary, trusting that the Lord strengthens and prospers them when they are faithful. They protect and give land to the Anti-Nephi-Lehies and people of Ammon, though this brings hardship. Under Moroni they preserve peace, build defenses, recover cities and lands, and resist efforts to subject them to Lamanite rule. They endure immense casualties, hunger, lack of provisions, and too few men, yet reclaim cities including Gid, Antiparah, Cumeni, Manti, Mulek, and Nephihah. Their history also includes peace, prosperity, humility, church and law being reestablished, and growth in strength and riches; but wickedness and internal conflict can cost them liberty. At the end, after peace is established, many depart from Zarahemla by Hagoth’s ships or go toward the land northward.

l: people of Anti-Nephi-Lehi, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The people of Anti-Nephi-Lehi are a people, originally Lamanites, converted unto the Lord. Their sore repentance leads them to fear sin, repent of murders, refuse arms, and bury their weapons deep in the earth as a testimony to God. They covenant not to shed their brethren’s blood, choosing to give their own lives instead; when war comes, they do not prepare or fight, and 1,005 are slain while calling on the Lord. Many Lamanites then join them as the people of God. At the Lord’s command they leave the land of Nephi, receive Jershon as an inheritance, and become known as the people of Ammon. Protected by the Nephites, they support Nephite armies with their substance. Though compassion later moves them to consider taking up arms, Helaman persuades them to keep their oath.

l: Lamanites, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The Lamanites are a people descended from Laman, Lemuel, the sons of Ishmael, and Ishmaelitish women. They are distinguished by shorn heads, skins girded about their loins, armor, and weapons including bows, arrows, stones, and slings; their dark skins are associated with a mark set upon their fathers. They bear a curse tied to transgression and rebellion, are cut off from the presence of the Lord, and inherit traditions that foster hatred, sin, violence, and opposition to the Nephites, though promises of salvation and future belief remain open to them. They inhabit the land of Nephi and surrounding wilderness, including areas divided from Nephite lands by a narrow wilderness. They repeatedly war against, kill, rob, plunder, capture, and take prisoners from the Nephites, while also suffering defeats, scattering, captivity, and loss of cities. Their armies are numerous and at times led by Zerahemnah, Amalickiah, Ammoron, and Zoramite chief captains. They capture and lose cities including Manti, Zeezrom, Cumeni, Antiparah, and Nephihah, attempt encirclements and poisoning, fortify cities, and eventually flee back toward the land of Nephi after reverses. A central development is conversion. Through Ammon, his brethren, records, preaching, and miracles, many Lamanites receive knowledge of God, repent, are baptized, become righteous, lay down or bury weapons, join the people of Anti-Nephi-Lehi or Ammon, and covenant for peace. Some refuse conversion or are stirred to anger by Amalekites, Amulonites, Zoramites, and dissenters, renewing war. Thus their history unfolds through inherited hostility and continual conflict, alongside repeated opportunities for repentance, faith, peace, and preservation for future generations.

l: king of the Lamanites, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: King of the Lamanites commands armies against the Nephites, appoints Amalickiah over obedient forces, then is stabbed by Amalickiah’s servant as Amalickiah falsely blames his servants.

l: contention, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: is_a disturbance [among the people] Contention begins among the people in the commencement of the fifth year of their reign because of Amlici's effort to become king. The people gather in separate bodies with much dispute and wonderful contentions.

l: establishing Amlici as king, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Amlici's followers endeavor to establish him as king, but the voice of the people rejects him. His followers then gather together and consecrate him as their king.

l: voice of the people, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The voice of the people is required by law to establish such matters. It comes against Amlici, so he is not made king over the people by that voice.

l: war between the Nephites and Amlicites, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: occurs_at hill Amnihu [east of the river Sidon] The war begins after Amlici commands his people to take up arms against the Nephites. The Nephites defeat the Amlicites, though many people on both sides are slain.

l: battle at the hill Amnihu, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Battle at hill Amnihu between Amlicites and Nephites begins when Amlicites attack; Alma leads the Nephites to defeat them.

l: crossing of the river Sidon, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: is_conducted_by Nephites [while fleeing from the Lamanites and Amlicites] The Nephites cross the river Sidon while the Lamanites and Amlicites attack them. Alma clears the west bank by throwing slain Lamanites into the river so his people can cross and continue fighting.

l: rights and privileges, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The people fear that if Amlici gains the voice of the people, he will deprive them of the rights and privileges of the church.

l: weapons of war, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Weapons of war are buried by Anti-Nephi-Lehi and repentant Lamanites, who throw them down and refuse to take them again.

l: hill Amnihu, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: is_east_of river Sidon The hill Amnihu is east of the river Sidon. The Amlicites attack the Nephites there, and many Nephites fall before the Lord strengthens them.

l: river Sidon, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The river Sidon runs by the land of Zarahemla in the south wilderness, bordering the land of Manti and a wilderness. Its depths contain bones of slain Lamanites and Amlicites. In battles, Nephites and Lamanites cross it: bodies are thrown into its waters, Zoram meets armies east of it, and Nephites hold both banks to encircle fleeing Lamanites.

l: land of Zarahemla, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The land of Zarahemla is a Nephite land containing the city of Zarahemla and, within its borders, the land of Ammonihah. The river Sidon runs by it, and a narrow wilderness separates it from the land of Nephi; it is the origin of a journey to Nephi. It is repeatedly a center of departure, arrival, preaching, settlement, military supply, and conflict. The sons of Mosiah and Ammon’s brethren depart from it, while the people of Anti-Nephi-Lehi seek it and are conducted there before settling in Jershon. Korihor preaches there and is brought before Alma and the chief judge. It receives captured Amalickiahites, sends inhabitants to the east wilderness, and supplies Helaman’s army. Lamanites and Amlicites attack near it; later Lamanites threaten and seize its lands. Pachus and dissenters take it, but Moroni and Pahoran recover it, restore peace, and leave defenders.

l: city of Zarahemla, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Zarahemla is a Nephite city, threatened with possession by Lamanites and Amlicites and home to an established church. Alma departs it for Gideon. Later dissenters hold it until Moroni and Pahoran defeat Pachus’s men, recover the city, and restore Pahoran to the judgment-seat.

l: the valley of Gideon, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The valley of Gideon, east of the river Sidon, is named for Gideon, slain by Nehor. After pursuing the Amlicites, Alma has the Nephites camp there; later he teaches the church in its city of Gideon.

l: land of Nephi, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The land of Nephi is a place nearly surrounded by water with Zarahemla, lying south of Nephite lands and running from the east sea to the west. It borders Zarahemla, contains wilderness where Lamanites live, and includes the city of Nephi, its chief city and site of the king’s palace. Owned by the Lamanites as possessions, it hosts a feast and is a destination for journeys, preaching, and military movements. Aaron, Ammon, and their brethren go there to teach in houses, streets, hills, temples, and synagogues, laboring and bringing forth much fruit amid journeyings and sufferings. After war, Lamanites return there, while Anti-Nephi-Lehi departs. Amalickiah travels there, gains command, and marches to its chief city; Moroni later names it Ammoron’s possession and demands his armies return there.

l: Alma, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Alma is a leader, prophet, teacher, preacher, and high priest over the church, consecrated by his father Alma. As chief judge and governor, he sees wickedness, inequality, and persecution in the church, becomes sorrowful, appoints Nephihah chief judge, delivers the judgment-seat to him, and devotes himself wholly to the high priesthood and preaching. He teaches repentance, faith in Christ, the Son of God, worship, prayer, the holy order, redemption, death, resurrection, judgment, and God’s rest. He explains the scriptures, knows Zeezrom’s thoughts through God’s Spirit, and calls people to humble themselves and not delay repentance. Imprisoned with Amulek, bound, beaten, mocked, and deprived, he seeks strength through faith in Christ, breaks his bonds, and survives the prison’s collapse. Believed to have prophecy, he inquires of the Lord, directs Zoram to the Lamanites, and preaches throughout the land. He confronts Korihor, testifies that church labor brought no gain, and declares that Korihor will be struck dumb. After ministering among the Zoramites and helping many repent, Alma returns to Zarahemla grieved by continuing iniquity, wars, bloodshed, contention, and hardened hearts. He has two sons and gives each a charge concerning righteousness.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Jerusalem is a great city in the land of the Lamanites, tied to the forefathers and Mary’s Son of God; Lamanites and others build it, and Aaron preaches there.

l: battle between the Lamanites and Amlicites, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: is_a battle [fought in the land of Zarahemla] The battle is fought in the land of Zarahemla in the fifth year of the reign of the judges. Many Lamanites and Amlicites are slain, and the slain Lamanites and Amlicites are cast into the waters of the river Sidon.

l: war, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: War is a long-running conflict involving the Nephites and the Lamanites, sometimes also marked by contentions among the Nephites. It brings thousands and tens of thousands of deaths, sending souls to the eternal world. Wars and contentions occur from the first through the fifteenth years of the reign of the judges; after years without conflict, the Lamanites invade again in the fourteenth year. The account returns to war in the eighteenth year, when the Nephites defend their lands, families, liberty, rights, and worship of God. Though reluctant to shed blood and taught to fight only to preserve life, the Nephites are compelled to continue contending for many years. Lamanites attack fortified Nephite cities, but Nephite preparations and the leadership of Moroni and Lehi bring victory. After Amalickiah's death, Ammoron continues the war, claiming rights to the government, while Moroni calls it an unjust war and seeks peace.

l: second Lamanite invasion, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: A second Lamanite army enters Nephite territory in the land of Zarahemla shortly after the battle there. Alma sends a numerous Nephite army, which slays many Lamanites and drives the remainder out of Nephite borders.

l: curse of God, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: result_from condemnation [those who are cursed bring it upon themselves] The curse is connected to the transgression and rebellion of Laman, Lemuel, the sons of Ishmael, and Ishmaelitish women. Those who mingle their seed with the Lamanites or are led away by the Lamanites receive the same curse, while the Amlicites bring the curse upon themselves through open rebellion.

l: mark, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: is_red red [on the foreheads of the Amlicites] The Lord God sets a mark upon the Lamanites and on those who mingle their seed with them, fight against Nephi and his seed, or depart from Nephi. The Amlicites set a red mark upon their own foreheads, fulfilling the word of God.

l: records, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The records brought out of the land of Jerusalem are believed by those called Nephites. The Nephites keep records that are true of their people and of the Lamanites.

l: the tradition of the Lamanites' fathers, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The tradition of the Lamanites' fathers is an incorrect, destructive set of teachings that contributes to Lamanite ignorance. Though some follow it while others are called Nephites for believing correct traditions and God’s commandments, the sons of Mosiah and missionaries expose its baseness, convince many, and help them learn it is not correct.

l: commandments of God, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The commandments of God are divine requirements declared and taught to people, including by Helaman, priests, high priests, Ammon, and Moroni. They follow God’s making known the plan of redemption, prohibit evil and sin, and attach a second, everlasting death to iniquity. Their central pattern is obedience and consequence: keeping them faithfully brings prosperity in the land, blessing, God’s continuing presence, and warning, direction, and deliverance; refusing them brings separation and being cut off from God’s presence, and may cause sacred things to be taken away. They are presented as forgotten by the people of Ammonihah, received daily by Lamoni’s people, kept zealously by the people of Ishmael, and required of the Nephites as a condition of prosperity. Moroni’s covenantal obedience also leads him to defend his country and resist iniquity.

l: Alma (father of Alma), The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Alma's father, a holy prophet, believed Abinadi's words, experienced a mighty change of heart, and preached to his fathers. Consecrated high priest, he established the church of God in Mormon near Nephi and baptized people in the waters of Mormon.

l: Nephihah, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Nephihah, a wise elder of the church, is appointed by Alma as the second chief judge through the people’s voice. He governs from the judgment-seat with power to enact and enforce laws, serves with perfect uprightness before God, and is Pahoran’s father.

l: high priesthood of the holy order of God, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The high priesthood of the holy order of God is a holy order received through holy calling and ordinance, after the order of the Only Begotten Son and prepared from eternity. After delivering the judgment-seat to Nephihah, Alma retained it and devoted himself to testimony, revelation, and prophecy.

l: the Spirit of the Lord, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The Spirit of the Lord, also called the Holy Spirit of God and Spirit of God, is one with God and Christ and knows all things. It reveals God’s word and wisdom to Alma, makes spiritual truth known, and is the source of revelation and prophecy. It testifies that the Son of God will come, confirms truth and faith, and calls Ammon to teach in the land of Ishmael. God gives people a portion of this Spirit to soften their hearts and enable correspondence with the Nephites. After Alma lays hands on his fellow laborers, the Holy Spirit fills them and prepares them for their work.

l: resurrection of the dead, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: The resurrection of the dead is the raising or coming forth of the dead, in which soul or spirit is reunited with the body in perfect form. Mortal bodies are restored as immortal and incorruptible, and all people, both just and unjust, will come forth at a time appointed by God. There is a temporal space between death and resurrection. It is brought to pass through the plan of redemption, the atonement, and the Son of God rising from the dead; Christ breaks the bands of death. After Christ’s coming, people are raised, brought into the presence of God, stand before the Son of God, and are judged according to their works, the law, and justice. It is taught by priests, Aaron, and the scriptures, and is preached with the Son of God. The people of Ammon hold hope in Christ and the resurrection, through which death is swallowed up by Christ’s victory.

l: remission of sins, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Remission of sins is expected by people through Christ and received from Lord Jesus Christ after a merciful plea amid anguish.

l: afflictions of the people, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Afflictions of the people arise from lost brethren, livestock, and grain destroyed by the Lamanites. Humble followers of God suffer for Christ’s sake; later Moroni, Helaman, and their men endure hunger, thirst, fatigue, while Lamanites murder people and carry women and children captive.

l: baptism, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
s: Baptism is performed by Alma, son of Alma, in the waters of Sidon and by Alma’s father in the waters of Mormon. It follows belief and is offered unto repentance, washing people from sins and showing willingness to repent and enter a covenant to keep God’s commandments. People are baptized, join the church of God, and about three thousand five hundred souls are baptized in the seventh year.

l: church, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma
